REGULATIONS N o 002/CMA/2026 OF
02/10/2026 RELATING TO THE
CAPITAL MARKET CORPORATE
GOVERNANCE
The Chief Executive Officer of the Capital
Market Authority of Rwanda;
Pursuant to the Constitution of the Republic
of Rwanda;
Pursuant to Law nº 057/2021 bis of
18/09/2021 establishing the Capital Market
Authority of Rwanda, especially in Article 9;
Having reviewed the capital market corporate
governance code n° 09, 2012;
After consideration and approval by the
Board of Directors of the Capital Market
Authority of Rwanda, in its meeting of
26/08/2024;
Issues the following Regulations:

CHAPTER ONE: GENERAL
PROVISIONS
Article One: Purpose of these Regulations
The purpose of these Regulations is to provide
minimum standards to ensure that companies
are directed and governed by the Board of
Directors supported by the management.
Article 2: Interpretation
In these Regulations:
(a) “auditor” means an external auditor
that is a member of the Institute of
Certified Public Accountants of
Rwanda;
(b) “audit engagement partner” means
a partner, or other individual
appointed by the auditor who is
responsible for the audit engagement
and its performance, and for the
auditor’s report that is issued on behalf
of the firm, and who, where required,
has the authority from a professional,
legal or regulatory body;

(c) “Authority” means the Capital
Market Authority of Rwanda;
(d) “Board of Directors charter” means
a document outlining responsibilities
of the Board of Directors, its powers,
Board of Directors’ committees and
their responsibilities, separation of
responsibilities between the Board of
Directors and the management,
policies and practices of the Board of
Directors;
(e) “code of conduct” means a company
policy document delineating expected
level of ethical behaviour from all
associated with the company and
expected standards of behaviour
including –
(i) confidentiality of information;
(ii) exhibiting company values in
every aspect of business
behaviour;

(iii)relationships with –
(A) government;
(B) officials;
(C) regulators;
(D) competitors;
(iv) whistleblowing and grievance
arrangements;
(v) use and care of company assets
and property;
(vi) disclosure of potential conflicts of
interest;
(vii) handling of external gifts and
donations;
(viii) observance of applicable laws
and regulations; and
(ix) behaviour towards stakeholders;
(f) “company secretary” means a
person appointed by a competent

authority and responsible for ensuring
that the company’s activities comply
with the legal provisions;
(g) “confidential information” means
all non-public information relating to
the company from whatever source;
(h) “corporate governance” means the
ethical and effective leadership of the
company for its direction and control;
(i) “director” means a member of the
Board of Directors, whether a
shareholder or not, being appointed by
shareholders to oversee the
management of a company;
(j) “engagement review partner” means
a partner or other individual appointed
by the auditor who is responsible for
the performance of the engagement
quality review including conducting
an objective evaluation of the
significant judgments made by the
engagement team and the conclusions
reached thereon that is completed on

or before the date of the engagement
report;
(k) “ESG” means a set of environmental,
social and governance matters which
companies consider;
(l) “executive director” means a person
who is appointed to the Board of
Directors and who concurrently holds
a senior management position in the
company;
(m) “general assembly” includes the
annual general meeting and
extraordinary general meetings of
shareholders;
(n) “immediate family member” means
a family member of a director or the
management to third degree;
(o) “independent director” means a
director who has no direct or indirect
material pecuniary relationship with
the capital market company, who is
free from any interest, position or
relationship which would be or would

appear to be an undue influence or
might cause bias in decision-making,
whether directly or indirectly;
(p) “related party” means, in relation to
a transaction or proposed transaction,
a person or entity that complies with
the following:
(i) to be a person or entity that will or
perceived to derive a material
financial or any other benefit from
the transaction;
(ii) to have a material financial or
other interest in another party to
the transaction;
(iii)to exercise control or joint control
or significant influence over a
party to the transaction;
(iv) to be a director, officer or trustee,
key management of another party

to, or person who will or may
derive a material financial benefit
from, the transaction, not being a
party or person that is–
(A) the company’s holding
company being a holding
company of which the
company is a wholly-
owned subsidiary;
(B) a wholly-owned subsidiary
of the company;
(C) a wholly-owned subsidiary
of a holding company of
which the company is also
a wholly-owned
subsidiary;
(v) to be an immediate family member
of another party to, or person who
will or may derive a material
financial or any other benefit from
the transaction;

(vi) to be otherwise directly or
indirectly materially interested in
the transaction;
(q) “internal control system” means a
coordinated set of policies,
procedures, tasks, behaviours and
rules that serve as the controls
governing the effectiveness of the
company’s organisational and
operational structure, including
reporting processes, the functions for
risk management, compliance and
internal audit;
(r) “issuer of securities” means a legal
entity that develops, registers and sells
securities to finance its operations.
Issuers may have a variety of legal
status;
(s) “listed company” means a company
whose securities in question have been
accepted for listing on an approved

stock exchange by the Authority;
(t) “listings rules” means rules as
contained in Rwanda Stock Exchange
rule book or other authorities rules as
applicable from time to time;
(u) “management” includes the Chief
Executive Officer or managing
director, executive directors and the
senior managers of the company
involved in the day-to-day activities of
the company;
(v) “material information” means all
information whose omission,
obscuring or misstatement could
reasonably be expected to influence
the assessment of a company’s value,
an investor’s decision or the price of
securities in the capital market;
(w) “non-executive director” means a
director who does not form part of the
management team of the company and

who is not an employee of the
company or affiliated with it, but who
can own shares in the company;
(x) “publish” means to put the document
or information on the company
website or through other means to
enable the public access;
(y) “share” means one of the equal parts
into which a company’s capital is
divided issued to every shareholder or
the company itself;
(z) “shareholder” means a person whose
name is entered on the share register
as the holder for the time being of one
share or more in the company;
(aa) “stakeholder” means an
individual or group of persons that
may affect or be affected by a
company’s operations, they include
investors, employees, customers,
suppliers, community, government
and regulators;

(bb) “unlisted company” means
the company whose securities in
question have not been accepted for
listing on stock exchange approved by
the Authority.
Article 3: Scope of application
These Regulations apply to –
(a) listed companies and issuers of
securities to the public or a section of
the public, regardless of the nature of
their business, their shareholders and
other stakeholders; and
(b) companies that intend to issue
securities to the public or section of
the public, public companies, State-
owned companies, private companies,
small and medium sized enterprises.

CHAPTER II: CORPORATE
GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK
Article 4: Governance of a company
(1) Every company is led by an ethical
and effective Board of Directors
which is accountable to the
shareholders, stakeholders, creditors
and employees of the company.
(2) The shareholders of each company are
responsible for the appointment of
competent and dedicated Directors.
Article 5: Companies in companies’ group
Parent or holding companies of company
groups adopt and monitor application of
governance policies and practices at the
individual entity level within the group to
ensure corporate governance best practices as
required by these Regulations are applied
across the whole group. Disclosure of the
group structure, including company capital
structure, control arrangements and

communications with group entities and
monitoring activities by the group Board of
Directors over group entities is required.
CHAPTER III: BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Article 6: Composition of the Board of
Directors
(1) The Board of Directors of a company
is composed of at least seven and at
most 11 directors depending on the
size, nature and complexity of the
operations of the company. However,
the Board of Directors of a small or
medium enterprise is composed of at
least three and at most five directors.
(2) The independent director is
compensated only through sitting
allowances.
(3) In the interest of accountability and
balance of power at least half of the
Board of Directors must comprise
non-executive directors, with at least

one third of the Board of Directors
being independent directors.
Article 7: Requirements for being an
independent director
An independent director must not –
(a) be, or have been in the last three years
employed by the company or its
subsidiaries;
(b) be nominated director representative
of a substantial shareholder of the
company or its subsidiaries;
(c) have immediate family ties with any
of the advisers, directors or senior
employees of the company or its
subsidiaries;

(d) be a significant provider of financial
capital to the company or its
subsidiaries or hold shares
representing more than 2% of the total
share capital or outstanding voting
power;
(e) have, or have had in the past three
years, a material business relationship
with the company or its subsidiaries,
whether directly, as a stakeholder or
shareholder, or through a directorship,
office, or senior employment with an
entity having such a relationship. A
shareholding in the company that falls
within the acceptable limits prescribed
under these Regulations shall not, on
its own, be treated as such a
relationship;
(f) be, or have been in the past three years
the designated auditor responsible for
the performance of the statutory audit
and must not have been a key member
of the audit team of the company or its
subsidiaries in the past three years;

(g) be, or have been during the past three
years a director or member of the
management of a significant customer
or supplier of the company or its
subsidiaries;
(h) be affiliated with any non-profit
organization that receives significant
funding from the company or its
subsidiaries;
(i) receive, or have received in the past
three years, an additional
remuneration from the company or its
subsidiaries other than the director’s
fee and that director’s fee does not
constitute a significant portion of their
annual income;
(j) participate in a share option plan or
pension plan or incentive scheme of
the company or its subsidiaries;

(k) be employed as an executive officer of
another company where the
company’s executives serve on that
company’s Board of Directors;
(l) hold a material interest in the
company or its subsidiaries either
directly or as a stakeholder,
shareholder, director, officer or senior
employee of a person who holds such
an interest;
(m) be a member of the immediate family
or be the executor, administrator or
personal representative of a deceased
or legally incapacitated person, of a
person who does not meet the criteria
provided for in other Sub-paragraphs
of this Article if they are a director of
the company;
(n) be identified in the annual report of the
company distributed to the

shareholders of the company as an
independent director; and
(o) have served on the Board of Directors
for a consecutive period of more than
nine years.
Article 8: Responsibilities of the Board of
Directors
The Board of Directors has the following
responsibilities:
(a) to ensure that all management
decisions are made in accordance with
prudent corporate governance
practices;
(b) to promote the success of the company
by directing, supervising and
controlling the company’s affairs. For
the avoidance of doubt, the Board of
Directors acts collectively and no
individual director has the power to
make binding decisions or to act
without agreement by or formal
delegation from the Board of
Directors;

(c) to act in good faith in a manner that the
director on reasonable grounds
believes to be in the best interest of the
company;
(d) to exercise care, diligence and skills
reasonably in different circumstances;
(e) to exercise power for proper purpose;
(f) to act in loyalty to the company, which
includes using company information
acquired by virtue of the director’s
position and company opportunities,
in the interest of the company and not
to gain personal benefit for the
director or another person or entity;
(g) to act with integrity, promote a
desirable culture, provide
entrepreneurial leadership and
direction to management and to
monitor the effectiveness of the ESG
and other policies and practices;

(h) to ensure high-quality governance
policies are applied, reviewed and
monitored, including if relevant,
across a broader company group
structure;
(i) to ensure clear division of
responsibilities between the Board of
Directors and those of management;
(j) to ensure decisions of the Board of
Directors take into account the
interests of stakeholders;
(k) to review, guide and approve strategy
that ensures that environmental and
social opportunities and risks are
taken into account to ensure the
company creates value and
contributes to sustainable
development;
(l) to ensure that the approved strategy is
expressed in a business plan and
budget with agreed targets and the
implementation of the business plan
and budget and progress against
targets are monitored and overseen;

(m) to manage the risks of the company by
establishing an effective risk
management framework and policies
in a way that supports the company in
achieving its strategic objectives;
(n) to ensure that a prudent and effective
internal control system exists,
adequate assurance functions and
services are established to monitor and
assess the effectiveness of such
internal controls;
(o) to oversee compliance with applicable
laws, regulations and non-binding
rules, codes of conduct and standards
that have been adopted by the
company;
(p) to establish, approve and publish a
code of conduct and Board of
Directors’ charter;
(q) to establish a written delegation of
powers framework, including Board
of Directors’ delegation of powers to
committees of the Board of Directors
and to the management as required,

without abdicating accountability and
a clear statement of powers the Board
of Directors reserves only unto itself;
(r) to establish a framework for
delegation of authority that articulates
the powers delegated to management
via the Chief Executive Officer and is
clear about the powers of the Chief
Executive Officer to further delegate;
(s) to annually set performance
requirements of the Chief Executive
Officer or Managing Director for
financial and operating goals;
(t) to review the Chief Executive Officer
or Managing Director and
management’s performance and
determine fair and responsible
remuneration;
(u) to oversee adequate succession
planning in place for executive
management and other key positions
to provide continuity in leadership;

(v) to ensure balance of the interests and
expectations of shareholders and other
stakeholders in the best interest of the
company over time;
(w) to ensure that the company issues
reports that enable shareholders and
other stakeholders to make an
informed assessment of the
company’s structure, governance,
strategy and risks, performance and
prospects of the company;
(x) to disclose any non-compliance with
these Regulations and the steps and
time frame to full compliance;
(y) to formulate policies, procedures and
guidelines which ensure that all
directors and senior management are
made fully aware of the requirements
of these Regulations;
(z) to perform any other responsibility
that contributes to the effective
performance of the company.

Article 9: Conduct and competence of
directors
(1) Directors have the following conduct
and competence:
(a) integrity in personal and
professional dealings;
(b) exercise of sound judgement in the
best interest of the company;
(c) sufficient working knowledge to
interpret and analyse financial
statements and understand the
financial implications of
decisions;
(d) business and industry knowledge
to effectively contribute as a
director;
(e) ability to exercise duties in a fair,
transparent, responsible and
accountable manner, and ability to
challenge management
constructively;

(f) be able and prepared to devote
sufficient time and effort to the
exercise of the duties;
(g) not hold directorships in more than
three Board of Directors of listed
public companies.
(2) A director adds value to the Board of
Directors and, bring independent and
objective judgment to bear on the
exercise of duties and decision making
regardless of whether classified as an
independent director or not.
(3) A director maintains confidentiality of
non-public information entrusted to
them in the course of their duties as
director.
(4) The Board of Directors approves a
process to obtain, outside legal or
other professional advice at the
company’s expense on any matter
deemed necessary for a director or the
Board of Directors to effectively
perform its duties.

Article 10: Quorum
The quorum for the meeting of the Board of
Directors is –
(a) one-third of independent directors;
and
(b) two directors who are executive
directors including the Chief
Executive Officer.
Article 11: Nomination, election and
appointment of directors
(1) The Nominating Committee oversees
the establishment of a formal and
transparent nomination process to
identify suitable director candidates
for election and appointment to the
Board of Directors by shareholders.
(2) The Nominating Committee requires a
person who seeks to be appointed as a
director to submit at least the
following information for

consideration:
(a) qualifications;
(b) skills and experience;
(c) current directorships or other
active involvement in other public
or private companies either listed
or unlisted companies;
(d) interests they have in the capital
market company, if any;
(e) any other affiliation that may
affect the director’s ability to
make independent and impartial
decisions, in the case of
independent directors; and
(f) a statement certifying that there
has not been in the last three years
or there is not currently any
disqualification from serving as a
director.

(3) Prior to nomination of a person who
seeks to be appointed as a director for
election or appointment, the
Nominating Committee
independently gathers information
and carry out verification on their
backgrounds and qualifications. The
information gathering ensures that the
person who seeks to be appointed as a
director is not disqualified from
serving as director under the law
governing companies.
(4) The Board of Directors provides to all
shareholders at least the information
provided for in Paragraph (2) as
submitted by the nominated person
who seeks to be appointed as a
director. Shareholders vote based on
this information.
(5) Upon election of a person as a
director, they are given letter of
appointment containing terms and
conditions for serving as director and
undergo a formal induction
programme as provided for in these
Regulations.

(6) The Nominating Committee reviews
annually whether the size and
composition of the Board of Directors
contribute to the Board of Directors’
effective discharge of duties and the
company’s strategic direction.
(7) Directors are nominated, elected and
appointed in accordance with the
principle of gender equality, ensuring
representation of different age groups
and consideration of their previous
professional background.
Article 12: Term of office of directors
(1) No term limit is set for directors of
listed companies generally. However,
if the independent director has been on
the Board of Directors for nine years,
the Audit Committee reassesses their
independence and recommends in
annual report if the independent
director may remain designated as
independent director.

(2) The Board of Directors discloses in
the annual report, the independent
directors and their years of service.
(3) To ensure continuity of operations, the
Board of Directors operates in such a
way that there is rotation of one-third
of its directors being replaced.
Article 13: Declaration of another
appointment
If any of the non-executive director or
independent director is offered an
appointment elsewhere, they inform the
Chairperson of the Nominating Committee
before any new appointments are accepted
and they include all appointments in the
declaration of interest’s register.
Article 14: Induction and ongoing
professional development
(1) To ensure that directorship is
professional, a company provides the
opportunities and funds for induction
and ongoing professional

development of directors.
(2) New directors are provided with
orientation as well as training on the
law, corporate governance, accounting
rules and other business matters.
(3) The orientation and training are
accompanied with site visits,
interviews with senior management
and attendance at conferences as may
be necessary to familiarise new
directors with the operations of the
company, its industry, current
financial position, strategy, risks and
business model.
(4) On a continuing basis and in any event
at least once a year, the directors
undertake a refresher course on the
latest developments in the relevant
industry, corporate governance,
relevant laws, accounting and tax
matters as offered by a reputable
service provider.

Article 15: Performance evaluation of the
Board of Directors
(1) The Board of Directors annually
undertakes the evaluation of its own
performance, that of the Chairperson,
individual directors and its
committees.
(2) The performance evaluation process is
overseen by the Nominating
Committee or a designated committee
as agreed by the Board of Directors
and is followed with improvement
plans.
(3) The Board of Directors may use an
independent service provider to
conduct a performance evaluation of
the Board of Directors, directors and
committees of the Board of Directors,
who would make recommendations
for improvements based on its
evaluation.
Article 16: Conflict of interests
(1) Directors, managers and employees
must avoid a conflict of interests.
Personal interests do not take

precedence over company interests.
(2) A company develops a conflict-of-
interest policy to be approved by the
Board of Directors, applicable by all
directors and employees and
published. The management ensures
that the conflicts of interests are
identified, disclosed, managed,
monitored and reported.
(3) A director, officer or senior manager
of the company, at least once a year or
immediately when changes take place,
must submit to the Board of Directors
a declaration of financial, economic
and other interests they held as well as
that of immediate family members to
the extent that these are known. This
information forms part of the register
of interests of the company.
Immediate disclosure is required by
every director, officer or senior
manager of any interest, direct or
indirect, in any transaction or
arrangement with the company.
Participation in the transaction or
arrangement is precluded.

(4) If a director or senior manager is a
related party in a transaction or
proposed transaction with the
company, they first disclose to the
Board of Directors the nature and
extent of the interest, and, where it
may be quantified, the monetary value
of such interest. The director or senior
manager does not participate in any
decision taking or seek to influence
any decision in the matter.
(5) The Board of Directors establishes
guidelines for overseeing business
transactions that occur between
related parties, in order to prevent
unfair or abusive treatment of any
party. The Board of Directors
develops, approves and publishes on
the company website a related-party
transactions policy, requiring all
transactions with the company to be
independent, on commercial terms
and conditions, and related-party
transactions be subject to review and
through approval processes and
publicly disclosed in the annual
report.

CHAPTER IV: BOARD MANAGEMENT
Article 17: Separation of the duties of the
President and the Chief Executive Officer
(1) To ensure appropriate balance of
power and accountability, the Chief
Executive Officer cannot be the
Chairperson of the Board of Directors.
(2) The Chairperson of the Board of
Directors must meet the criteria for
being classified as an independent
director.
(3) The division of responsibilities
between the Chairperson of the Board
of Directors and the Chief Executive
Officer is established and provided for
in writing in the Board of Directors’
charter.
(4) In the responsibilities of the
Chairperson of Board of Directors,
includes the following:

(a) to lead the Board of Directors to
ensure that it is ethical and
effective and that it maintains high
standards of governance;
(b) to guide the development of the
annual work plan of the Board of
Directors and the setting of its
agenda for each meeting;
(c) to ensure that the Board of
Directors receives accurate, timely
and clear information to discharge
its duties;
(d) to encourage constructive working
relationships between the Board of
Directors and management;
(e) to ensure the effective
contribution of non-executive
directors during and outside of
Board of Directors’ meetings to
facilitate robust and informed
oversight and decision-making.

Article 18: Governance advisory duties to
the Board of Directors
(1) A company employs a professionally
qualified company secretary to
perform the duties of governance
advisory as provided for in the law
governing companies and to provide
support and guidance to the Board of
Directors and directors on their
responsibilities.
(2) In the event that the Board of
Directors cannot justify the cost of a
full-time in-house company secretary,
the function may be performed by an
external service provider subject to the
provider being independent and not
also the auditor, company lawyer, or
other advisor to the Board of
Directors.
(3) The company secretary keeps an
annual record of the company’s
compliance with these Regulations
and all other relevant laws.

Article 19: Relationship between the Board
of Directors and the Chief Executive
Officer
(1) The Board of Directors appoints the
Chief Executive Officer and the Chief
Executive Officer is accountable to it.
If necessary, the Board of Directors
has the authority to dismiss the Chief
Executive Officer after following due
process.
(2) The Board of Directors empowers the
Chief Executive Officer to lead the
management team and to implement
and execute strategy, risk
management, company policies and
operational planning.
(3) Annually the Board of Directors
formally evaluates the performance of
the Chief Executive Officer against
previously agreed performance
measures and targets.
(4) The Board of Directors may instruct
management to attend its meetings as
standing invitees or on an ad hoc-
basis, as required, to provide

information considered necessary to
effectively deliberate on decisions and
perform its duties.
Article 20: Chief Executive Officer and
management
(1) The Chief Executive Officer ensures
that day-to-day business affairs of the
company are appropriately managed
and monitored, that key management
functions are headed by an individual
with the necessary competence and
authority to fulfil the specified role
and that these functions are adequately
resourced.
(2) The Chief Executive Officer develops
and recommends to the Board of
Directors a long-term vision and
strategy of the company for approval,
that will generate satisfactory levels of
shareholder value and positive
reciprocal relations with relevant
stakeholders.
(3) The Chief Executive Officer develops
and recommends to the Board of
Directors annual business plans and
budgets to support the company’s

long-term strategy, for approval.
(4) The Chief Executive Officer
maintains a positive and ethical work
environment conducive to attracting,
retaining and motivating a diverse
group of employees and management.
(5) The Chief Executive Officer and
management ensure proper processes
for identification and assessment of
the risks to the achievement of the
company strategies, and report
regularly to the Board of Directors on
the management and mitigation of
these risks.
(6) Leadership of the risk management
function must be assigned to an officer
experienced in risk management.
CHAPTER V: BOARD COMMITTEES
Article 21: Committees of the Board of
Directors
(1) In order to fulfil its responsibilities,

the Board of Directors establishes the
following committees and appoints
their members from among its own
directors:
(a) Nominating Committee;
(b) Remuneration Committee;
(c) Audit Committee.
(2) The committees of the Board of
Directors must have a written and
publicly disclosed terms of reference
that addresses membership, role and
responsibilities, meeting procedures
and quorum for decisions. The terms
of reference of each committee clearly
state which areas are delegated to the
committee.
(3) Recommendations of the committees
are subject to the decision of the Board
of Directors.
(4) The Board of Directors may establish
other committees in addition to those
provided in Paragraph (1), to support
its work.

Article 22: Delegation of power to
committees of the Board of Directors
Subject to the law governing companies, the
Board of Directors is entitled to delegate its
power to its committees without abdicating
accountability.
Article 23: Nominating Committee
(1) The Nominating Committee is
composed of at least three non-
executive directors, a majority of
whom must be independent and its
Chairperson must be an independent
director.
(2) The Nominating Committee ensures a
robust and transparent process for the
nomination, election and appointment
of directors.
(3) A person nominated by the
Nominating Committee is subject to
an approval by the Board of Directors

before being elected by shareholders.
Article 24: Remuneration Committee
(1) The Remuneration Committee is
composed of at least three directors,
including at least one independent
director.
(2) The Remuneration Committee
oversees the remuneration of
management and non-executive
directors as well as a company-wide
policy on employee remuneration. If
the size of the Board of Directors is an
impediment in carrying out its duties,
this role may be undertaken by the
Nominating Committee.
Article 25: Audit Committee
(1) The Board of Directors determines
duties of the Audit Committee
compliant with the Law governing
companies, these Regulations and
with Board charter.

(2) The Audit Committee is composed of
at least three directors, the majority of
whom are independent directors.
(3) The Chairperson of the Audit
Committee must –
(a) be independent director;
(b) be a financial expert;
(c) have the relevant qualifications
and experience in auditing,
finance or accounting; and
(d) be a member of a professional
body in good standing.
(4) The Board of Directors ensures that a
member of the Audit Committee is
financially literate and has the
required accounting, auditing or
related knowledge and experience for
the execution of the duties of the
Committee.

(5) The Audit Committee meets at least
once every quarter and as often as is
necessary for the effective discharge
of its duties, especially with regard to
reporting responsibilities.
CHAPTER VI: REMUNERATION AND
REWARD
Article 26: Remuneration and reward
policy
(1) A company must have a formal and
transparent policy on fair and
responsible remuneration for
management and company-wide
employee remuneration. Staff are not
involved in deciding their own
remuneration.
(2) The Remuneration Committee
recommends for Board of Directors
approval a remuneration and reward
policy which attracts, retains and
motivates management to run the
company successfully, whilst being
fair and responsible.

(3) The performance-related
remuneration and reward form a
significant proportion of the total
remuneration of management and
designed to incentivise high
performance without excessive risk-
taking. Performance measures address
economic or financial performance,
governance, environmental and social
performance dimensions.
(4) The rewards for non-executive
director reflect the time commitment,
responsibilities and commensurate
with being a professional.
(5) The Remuneration Committee must
be aware of what remuneration and
reward comparable companies are
paying and take account of relative
performance.
CHAPTER VII: RISK MANAGEMENT,
INTERNAL CONTROL AND AUDIT

Article 27: Risk management
(1) The Board of Directors is responsible
for an effective risk management
system or framework and ensures the
company develops and executes a
comprehensive and robust system of
risk management including effective
information technology governance.
(2) The Board of Directors –
(a) determines the overall risk
appetite for the company and
communicate this to management;
(b) receives regular reports on risk
management and monitor the
effectiveness of the risk
management system; and
(c) regularly reviews, considers and
reports on foreseeable risks and
that there are appropriate risk
responses in place.

(3) The risk framework should include the
systematic and continuous
identification, assessment and
prioritisation of material risks as well
as the design and implementation of
effective and efficient risk responses.
The company uses tools for
performance measurement of risks
and risk mitigation.
(4) The management ensures the effective
operation of the risk management
system.
(5) In large companies and companies
with more complex business models
and activities, the Board of Directors
should consider the introduction of a
separate committee to monitor and
oversee risk.
Article 28: Internal controls of a company
(1) The Audit Committee ensures that
management establishes and
maintains a sound system of internal
controls of a company that effectively
manages risks.

(2) The Audit Committee, at least
annually, review the adequacy of the
company’s internal financial controls,
operational and compliance controls,
and risk management policies and
systems established by management
of the company.
Article 29: Internal audit of a company
(1) A listed company must have a well-
resourced and competent internal
audit function to provide an
independent and objective assurance
to the Board of Directors on the
efficiency and effectiveness of
company operations, including the
evaluation of risk management,
control and governance processes.
(2) The internal audit function has an
Internal Audit Charter, a broad scope
of work to investigate all levels of the
company and to be independent from
management. The internal auditor
reports primarily to the chairperson of
the audit committee and

administratively to the Chief
Executive Officer.
Article 30: Internal audit plan
The internal audit plan includes –
(a) a review of compliance with laws; and
(b) regulations and relevant company
policies.
Article 31: Auditor of a company
(1) The Audit Committee recommends to
the Board of Directors on the
appointment, re-appointment and
removal of the auditor of the company
and approval of their remuneration
and the terms of engagement.
Shareholders approve the appointment
of an auditor.
(2) The auditor and the audit engagement
partner are independent, well qualified
to carry out their duties, and be free of
actual and perceived conflicts of

interests. Audit firms must not be
engaged in accounting or other non-
audit services that place them in a
position where they audit the output of
their own work.
(3) The audit engagement partner, the
audit team and the engagement review
partner must be independent from the
company being audited and not hold
shares in the company.
(4) The external audit engagement partner
for a listed company is replaced every
five years.
Article 32: Responsibilities of the Audit
Committee
The responsibilities of the Audit Committee
are the following:
(a) to recommend to the Board of
Directors the appointment and

removal of the head of internal audit
of the company as well as the
remuneration for this position;
(b) approves the internal audit scope and
plan prior to the commencement of
each financial year;
(c) to review the internal audit report and
monitor management’s
responsiveness to internal audit
findings;
(d) to assess, at least once a year, the
effectiveness of the internal audit
function, including the adequacy of its
resources.
(e) to review annually the competence,
independence and objectivity of the
auditor;
(f) to meet with the auditor at least once a
year, in the absence of the
management.
CHAPTER VIII: SHAREHOLDER AND
STAKEHOLDER RELATIONS

Article 33: Fostering shareholder
relationships
(1) The management of a company
informs shareholders as to their rights
and responsibilities and actively
promotes their exercises, to foster
shareholders’ relationships.
(2) The company ensures the equitable
treatment of all shareholders,
including minority and foreign
shareholders as follows:
(a) shareholders of the same class
have the same rights on voting,
subscription, and transfer of
shares;
(b) to have a clearly articulated and
published policy on treatment of
minority shareholder rights
including changes of control,
disposal of substantially all of the
assets of the company and in
engagement with the company;
(c) shareholders receive adequate
notice and information pertaining

to the agenda for the general
assembly and are permitted to
participate and vote at the
assembly;
(d) holders of securities of the same
type and class have equal access to
information.
(3) A company releases information
equally to shareholders. If information
is inadvertently released to selected
shareholders only, a company makes
the same disclosure publicly to other
shareholders as soon as practically
possible and reports the matter to the
Authority immediately.
(4) The Board of Directors oversees the
provisions of Paragraphs (1), (2) and
(3) and ensures engagement in formal
and informal communication with
shareholders at a general assembly
and at other times through written
communication or other means as is
necessary to enable shareholders to –

(a) make investment decisions and
exercise voting rights on an
informed basis; and
(b) contribute constructively in
engagements with the company,
including providing input and
raising concerns.
Article 34: General Assembly
(1) A company encourages greater
shareholders attendance and
participation at the General Assembly
by allowing them the opportunity to
communicate their views on various
matters affecting the company.
(2) Documents related to the annual
General Assembly are posted on the
company website, including agenda,
registration process, voting rules,
proposed resolutions, and all
information related to proposed
resolutions.
(3) The General Assembly takes a
separate resolution on each

substantially separate issue.
(4) The company does not bundle
resolutions unless the resolutions are
interdependent and linked to form one
significant proposal.
(5) The information provided about the
agenda items for the General
Assembly are detailed to allow
shareholders to vote in an informed
way. The agenda is presented in the
order that items are addressed at the
General Assembly.
(6) Shareholders may be allowed to
participate in the General Assembly
and to vote remotely via electronic
access. The company makes the
appropriate provisions in its articles of
association to allow for electronic
general assemblies and in absentia
voting methods. Methods for voting
and participating in the General
Assembly in absentia are explained to
shareholders and provided with the
notice of the assembly.

(7) The outcome and proceedings of the
General Assembly are recorded in
minutes which are published on the
company’s website or through other
means for accessibility by
stakeholders of the company within
ten days from the General Assembly.
(8) Chairpersons of committees of Board
of Directors must be present at annual
General Assembly and available to
address questions. The auditor must
also be present to address
shareholders’ queries about the
conduct of audit, the preparation and
content of the auditors’ report.
(9) The agenda of the annual General
Assembly provides for time of asking
questions to the Chairperson of the
Board of Directors, the chairpersons
of the committees of the Board of
Directors and the external auditor.
Article 35: Voting in the General Assembly
(1) In establishing the voting procedures

and rights for a company, the principle
of “one share, one vote” guides every
company. Within a class of shares, all
shareholders have the same voting
rights. Information regarding the
voting rights of all classes of shares
must be available to current and
potential shareholders.
(2) Proxy voting rules must be simple,
easy to follow and provided with the
notice and materials for the annual
General Assembly to facilitate voting
by shareholders.
(3) Chairperson of the Board of Directors
explains to shareholders their voting
rights and procedures so that they may
assert their rights in the General
Assembly.
Article 36: Stakeholder engagement and
social and environmental responsibilities
(1) The Board of Directors ensures the
establishment and effectiveness of a

formal stakeholder policy and
processes that encourage engagement
with the company and its
management, identifies key
stakeholders, considers their material
needs, interests and expectations and
reports on these processes.
(2) To make ethical and responsible
decisions, the company –
(a) complies with its legal obligations,
and, must know and consider the
reasonable expectations of its key
stakeholders;
(b) develops policies that ensure the
health, safety, dignity and well-
being of its employees and
customers;
(c) ensures that measures are put in
place for the prevention, detection
and responses to fraud and
corruption; and
(d) mitigates the negative
consequence of its operations on
the environment and the

community within which it
operates.
(3) The Board of Directors is accountable
for the efficiency and effectiveness of
the provision of Paragraph (2).
Article 37: Whistle-blowing and grievance
mechanisms
(1) The Board of Directors oversees the
establishment and effectiveness of
mechanisms for whistle-blowing and
grievances to ensure that employees,
suppliers, customers, affected
communities and other stakeholders
are able to raise concerns on a
confidential basis about any suspected
or actual non-compliance, fraud or
other misconducts.
(2) A company informs stakeholders
about the whistle-blowing
mechanisms in an understandable
format and language.
(3) A company ensures that those who
report in good faith are protected from
negative repercussions as a result of
the reporting.

CHAPTER IX: INFORMATION
DISCLOSURE AND TRANSPARENCY
Article 38: Information disclosure
(1) A corporate governance framework
ensures that timely and accurate
disclosure to stakeholders is made on
all material matters regarding the
company, including –
(a) its financial and non-financial
situation;
(b) its strategy and risk management;
(c) its business model;
(d) its performance;
(e) its ownership; and
(f) its environmental and social
matters.
(2) The company and the Board of
Directors keep pace with changes on

the expected standards for company
reporting that evolve continually.
(3) A company abides the disclosure
policy by publication of a
comprehensive, understandable and
balanced annual report. The company
also makes regular use of its website
for timely disclosure of information.
The website must be easily accessible
and contain regularly updated
information, including annual reports,
interim reports, investor briefings,
company policies, Board of Directors
and Board committee charters, and
other documents.
Article 39: Information disclosure to
shareholders and stakeholders
(1) The Board of Directors establishes
policies and processes that are
practical and in accordance with
generally accepted best practices. The
policies ensure full, fair, accurate and
timely disclosure of all material
information to shareholders and to

stakeholders.
(2) The Board of Directors oversees
enforcement of quality reporting and
company disclosure policies.
(3) Material information relevant to the
value of shares or to investors must be
published immediately.
(4) The annual report of a company –
(a) identifies the major shareholders
of the company including
beneficial shareholders, their
shareholdings, and the key
stakeholders identified by the
company;
(b) identifies the audited financial
statements, a balanced view of
relevant financial and non-
financial information, including
strategy, the business model, risk
management, performance,
ownership, governance and

control of the company;
(c) identifies a discussion of the
significant or material
environmental and social risks and
opportunities and the company’s
responses to these matters;
(d) enables stakeholders to make an
informed assessment of the overall
performance of the company and
its longer-term prospects; and
(e) identifies a clear statement of
directors’responsibility for the
information provided.
(5) The Board of Directors ensures that
the financial statements present a true
and fair view of the financial position,
and performance of the company and
they comply fully with International
Financial Accounting Standards.
(6) Financial statements and accounts of a
company are audited in accordance
with International Standards on
Auditing. A company provides

assurance on the non-financial
information presented in the annual
report. The assurance is provided by a
competent professional assessor or
assessors who apply best international
assurance standards.
Article 40: Confirmation by the Board of
Directors of commitments made by
directors
The commitment of each director of the
company to ethical and effective leadership
and good governance are confirmed by the
Board of Directors in a statement to be
included in the annual report.
Article 41: Disclosure of interests of
directors and management
The Board of Directors ensures that the
following in relation to the interests of
directors and management are disclosed in the
annual report:
(a) the interests of directors and
management in the equity or debt
securities of the company or a

subsidiary as provided for in relevant
laws, interests in the company’s shares
and all material related party
transactions;
(b) the annual report of the company
discloses particulars on a contract–
(i) subsisting during or at the end of
the financial year in which a
director is issuer or was materially
interested, either directly or
indirectly, or, if there has been no
such contract, a statement of that
fact; and
(ii) for the provision of services to the
group by a controlling shareholder
or any of its subsidiaries.
Article 42: Disclosure of information
regarding directors
With regards to the directors, the following
information is disclosed in the company’s

annual report:
(a) the category of each director as
executive, non-executive or
independent director;
(b) qualifications, work experience and
occupations of each director as well as
other Board of Director’s positions
being held;
(c) the target set for gender equality
representation on the Board of
Directors and progress made to
achieving this target;
(d) each director’s period of service on the
Board of Directors;
(e) a statement of each director’s
attendance at Board of Directors and
its committee meetings and the total
meetings to be attended;
(f) other directorships held by each
director currently and the preceding
five years.

Article 43: Disclosure of information
regarding Board committees
In relation to the Board committees, the Board
of Directors discloses in the company’s
annual report –
(a) the chairperson of the committee,
members of the committee, their
qualifications, experience, and
independence if applicable;
(b) role of the committee, its
responsibilities and its significant
activities in the year; and
(c) the number of the committee meetings
and attendance of each director.
Article 44: Disclosure of duties and
responsibilities of the Nominating
Committee
The Nominating Committee discloses in the
company’s annual report how it executed its
duties and responsibilities, including the
activities and process the committee has

followed in arriving at recommendations for
nominations to the Board of Directors and the
process for inducting new directors.
Article 45: Disclosure of the functioning of
the Audit Committee
The Audit Committee discloses in the
company’s annual report how it has
performed its duties, including –
(a) oversight of financial and non-
financial reporting;
(b) the extent of non-audit services
provided by the auditors during the
year under review;
(c) the committee’s view on the
effectiveness of the Chief Finance
Officer and the finance function;
(d) the committee’s view on the
effectiveness of the internal control
system and the internal audit function
of the company; and

(e) the independence of the external
auditor.
Article 46: Disclosure of remuneration
policy
The Remuneration Committee discloses the
company remuneration policy, level and mix
of remuneration, and the procedure for setting
remuneration for the Board of Directors and
management in the company’s annual report.
The disclosure enables investors to
understand the link between remuneration and
performance.
Article 47: Disclosure of sustainability,
non-financial information, stakeholder
engagement and social and environmental
responsibilities
In relation to reporting on sustainability or
non-financial information, stakeholder
engagement and company social and
environmental responsibilities, the Board of
Directors ensures the disclosure of the
following in the company’s annual report:

(a) identification of any specific
framework the company used to guide
its sustainability practices and
reporting;
(b) the risks and opportunities associated
with environmental and social factors
that may affect the performance of the
company;
(c) the steps that the company has
taken to manage these risks and
opportunities, including specific
targets and performance
indicators;
(d) the company’s performance against
key selected social and environmental
targets and performance indicators.
Article 48: Disclosure of the grievance and
whistle-blowing mechanism
The company’s annual report discloses if the
company has established a grievance and
whistle-blowing mechanism, the general
themes of complaints made, how these have

been addressed by the company and the
number of any outstanding complaints.
Article 49: Disclosure of the Board of
Directors’ charter and terms of reference
for Board committees
The company ensures that the Board of
Directors’ charter and the terms of reference
for each committee of the Board of Directors
and other relevant documents and policies,
including the annual report, are disclosed and
accessible on the company’s website. The
company uses the website to disclose relevant
updated company and governance
information.
CHAPTER X: FINAL PROVISIONS
Article 50: Repealing provision
The capital market corporate governance code
n° 09, 2012 is repealed.

Article 51: Language provision
These Regulations were drafted in English.
Article 52: Entry into force
These Regulations come into force on the date
of their publication in the Official Gazette of
the Republic of Rwanda.
